scenes.head: Solvency and leverage
scenes.sub: Measure how far a business is financed by borrowing and how easily it carries the cost: debt and leverage ratios, interest and EBITDA coverage, net debt to EBITDA, leases and vendor finance as debt, and what to do when equity turns negative.

segs.say: Solvency and leverage. Measure how far a business is financed by borrowing and how easily it carries the cost: debt and leverage ratios, interest and EBITDA coverage, net debt to EBITDA, leases and vendor finance as debt, and what to do when equity turns negative.

scenes.head: You will be able to

segs.say: Calculate the debt ratio, liabilities to equity, debt to equity, debt to capital and the equity multiplier, and explain how they relate.
Calculate interest coverage, EBITDA coverage and net debt to EBITDA, and interpret them for a lender.
Identify what counts as debt, including vendor finance such as an instalment plan and, as an adjustment, operating lease liabilities under ASC 842.
Adjust leverage and coverage ratios for leases consistently, so that debt and earnings are measured on the same basis.
Explain why debt to equity and return on equity lose their meaning when equity is negative, using Starbucks.

scenes.head: At the end of 2026 Lantern was financed mostly by Ana: equity of $42,387 against $30,000 of loans (the Coastline note and the van note).

segs.say: At the end of 2026 Lantern was financed mostly by Ana: equity of $42,387 against $30,000 of loans (the Coastline note and the van note). By the end of 2027 its equity had grown to $62,818, but it also owed $65,250 of interest-bearing debt and $173,379 of lease liabilities for the two cafés. Coastline’s credit officer has a second question after liquidity: how much of Lantern now belongs, in effect, to its lenders and landlords, and how comfortably does it earn their interest?

scenes.head: Solvency is the ability to meet all obligations over the long run, not just those due this year.

segs.say: Solvency is the ability to meet all obligations over the long run, not just those due this year. A business is solvent when its assets are worth more than everything it owes and when its earnings can carry the cost of its debt. Leverage (in the UK, gearing) is the use of borrowed money to finance the business. Leverage is not bad in itself: interest is fixed, so when the business earns more than the debt costs, the owners keep the difference. But fixed payments must be made in bad years too, so leverage magnifies losses as well as gains, and every lender asks how much there is.

scenes.head: Solvency ratios come in two families.

segs.say: Solvency ratios come in two families. Leverage ratios compare stocks on the balance sheet: how much of the assets is financed by liabilities or debt rather than by equity. Coverage ratios compare flows: how many times the year’s earnings cover the interest, or how many years of earnings the debt represents. A lender wants both, because a business can have little debt and weak earnings, or a lot of debt and strong earnings.
Lantern’s leverage and coverage (fictional)

scenes.head: Every leverage measure rose and every coverage measure fell.

segs.say: Every leverage measure rose and every coverage measure fell. Liabilities went from 54.8% to 80.8% of total assets, and for every dollar of equity Lantern now has $4.22 of liabilities rather than $1.21. Interest coverage fell from 31.43 to 11.39 times. Lantern held more cash than debt at the end of 2026 (negative net debt); a year later its debt exceeded its cash by $58,719.

scenes.head: Two different stories sit inside those numbers.

segs.say: Two different stories sit inside those numbers. Interest-bearing debt a little more than doubled, from $30,000 to $65,250, and debt to equity rose modestly, from 0.71 to 1.04. Total liabilities rose more than fivefold, from $51,289 to $265,065, and almost two-thirds of the 2027 total is one item: the cafés’ lease liabilities. Whether leases are debt is therefore the most important judgement in Lantern’s solvency analysis, and this lesson takes it slowly.

scenes.head: Say which “debt” you mean

segs.say: Say which “debt” you mean. Analysts use “debt” for at least three things: total liabilities, interest-bearing debt, and interest-bearing debt plus lease liabilities. Lantern’s 2027 “debt to equity” is 4.22, 1.04 or 3.80 depending on the choice. None is wrong; mixing them is. This course uses interest-bearing debt unless it says otherwise, and calls the first ratio liabilities to equity.

chapters.title: Leverage ratios and how they connect

scenes.head: The leverage ratios all compare the two ways a business finances its assets: by owing (liabilities) or by owning (equity).

segs.say: The leverage ratios all compare the two ways a business finances its assets: by owing (liabilities) or by owning (equity). Because total assets = total liabilities + equity, they carry much the same information and can be converted into each other:
Equity multiplier = (Total assets)/Equity = 1 + (Total liabilities)/Equity = 1/(1 − Debt ratio)

Lantern 2027: 1 + 4.22 = 5.22, and 1 ÷ (1 − 0.808) = 5.22. The equity multiplier says Lantern controls $5.22 of assets for each dollar of equity; it reappears in the DuPont analysis of return on equity in module 3. The debt-to-capital ratio uses interest-bearing debt only: of the long-term funding provided by lenders and owners together, how much came from lenders? Lantern’s rose from 41.4% to 50.9%.

scenes.head: Which liabilities matter?

segs.say: Which liabilities matter? Trade payables, wages, taxes and unearned revenue are owed, but they arise from operating and they carry no interest; a lender worries most about claims that rank alongside its own and charge interest. Lantern’s 2027 liabilities split three ways: $65,250 of interest-bearing debt (24.6%), $173,379 of lease liabilities (65.4%) and $26,436 of operating liabilities (10.0%).
Lantern’s interest-bearing debt at 31 December 2027 (fictional)

scenes.head: Lantern bought its cold-brew brewer on the supplier’s plan: 24 monthly payments of $1,050, $25,200 in all, for a machine whose cash price is $24,000.

segs.say: Lantern bought its cold-brew brewer on the supplier’s plan: 24 monthly payments of $1,050, $25,200 in all, for a machine whose cash price is $24,000. It recorded the brewer and an instalment note at $24,000, and the $1,200 difference is interest, spread over the plan at its implied interest rate (F04 found it cheaper than Coastline’s 7.2% loan). The supplier is a lender in all but name, and the plan is interest-bearing debt with a repayment schedule. Vendor financing of this kind must be counted with the bank loans; had Lantern recorded it with its accounts payable, its debt ratios would look lower than its real borrowing.

chapters.title: Coverage: can earnings carry the debt?

scenes.head: Interest coverage (times interest earned) divides EBIT by interest expense.

segs.say: Interest coverage (times interest earned) divides EBIT by interest expense. EBIT is used because interest is paid out of earnings before tax; for Lantern, which has no income outside its operations, EBIT is operating income. Lantern’s fell from 37,716 ÷ 1,200 = 31.43 to 32,787 ÷ 2,879 = 11.39. EBITDA coverage adds back depreciation and amortisation, which use no cash in the year, and fell less steeply, from 35.43 to 18.27. Because both earnings and interest are flows over the same period, coverage ratios are not distorted by 2026’s ten months.

scenes.head: Two cautions.

segs.say: Two cautions. First, 2026’s EBIT was earned before Ana took any salary; the $48,000 she was paid in 2027 alone is larger than 2027’s EBIT, so 2026’s 31.43 flatters the business. Second, coverage counts interest, not principal. $51,091 of Lantern’s debt principal falls due in 2028 (the $24,000 line may be renewed, but the bank need not renew it), more than the $42,231 its 2027 EBITDA would leave after interest and tax. A lender looking at repayments as well uses a debt-service measure, comparing cash flow with interest plus scheduled principal.

scenes.head: Net debt to EBITDA asks how many years of EBITDA would repay the debt, net of cash.

segs.say: Net debt to EBITDA asks how many years of EBITDA would repay the debt, net of cash. Net debt is debt minus cash; Lantern’s was −$12,940 at the end of 2026 (more cash than debt) and $58,719 at the end of 2027, or 1.12 times EBITDA. Because it divides a balance by a flow, a part-year needs annualising: 2026’s ten-month EBITDA of $42,516 is $51,019 a year, giving −0.25 rather than −0.30. Lenders often set a maximum for this ratio in loan agreements, and define both sides carefully.

scenes.head: An operating lease commits the lessee to fixed payments for years, like a loan used to buy the asset.

segs.say: An operating lease commits the lessee to fixed payments for years, like a loan used to buy the asset. Since ASC 842 (effective for public companies for periods beginning after 15 December 2018, and for other entities three years later), lessees record that commitment: a right-of-use asset and a lease liability at the present value of the payments. Lantern’s cafés added $202,255 of each on 1 March 2027, discounted at 7.2%; by the year end the liability was $173,379. The liability is on the balance sheet, so it is already in the debt ratio and liabilities to equity. Whether it also belongs in “debt” is the analyst’s choice: ASC 842 itself characterises operating lease liabilities as operating liabilities rather than debt, so adding them to debt is an adjustment the analyst makes, and states, to see the business’s fixed commitments in full.

scenes.head: Operating leases in the statements under ASC 842 and IFRS 16

segs.say: Operating leases in the statements under ASC 842 and IFRS 16. Under US GAAP an operating lease’s cost is a single lease expense within income from continuing operations (Lantern’s Operating Lease Cost, $4,000 a month, $40,000 for ten months). The interest on the liability is inside that cost, so it is not in interest expense, EBIT is after it, and the payments are operating cash outflows. IFRS 16, effective for annual periods beginning on or after 1 January 2019, has a single lessee model: apart from leases of 12 months or less and of low-value assets, every lease is accounted for like a purchase on credit, with depreciation of the right-of-use asset and interest on the liability. The same café would therefore show higher EBIT and EBITDA, and more interest, under IFRS than under US GAAP. Compare across the two frameworks only after adjusting.

scenes.head: If the lease liability is counted as debt, the income statement must be adjusted to match, or the ratios mix two bases.

segs.say: If the lease liability is counted as debt, the income statement must be adjusted to match, or the ratios mix two bases. Treat the lease as a loan throughout: split the $40,000 lease cost into its interest part, $11,124 (the accretion on the liability), and its amortisation part, $28,876. Move the interest below EBIT into interest expense, and add the amortisation to depreciation and amortisation.
Lantern 2027, with and without the leases as debt

scenes.head: The adjustment changes the picture more than any other in Lantern’s analysis.

segs.say: The adjustment changes the picture more than any other in Lantern’s analysis. Interest coverage falls from 11.39 to 3.14: once the cafés’ rent is treated as financing, nearly a third of Lantern’s earnings before financing costs go to its lenders and landlords. Net debt to EBITDA rises from 1.12 to 2.51. The unadjusted figures are not wrong, but they leave out a five-year commitment that is as fixed as a loan’s.

scenes.head: One detail of the adjustment matters for comparisons.

segs.say: One detail of the adjustment matters for comparisons. It keeps ASC 842’s amortisation figure ($28,876), which early in a lease is below straight-line depreciation of the right-of-use asset, because the liability’s interest is highest at the start. Under IFRS 16 the same café would depreciate the asset straight-line, 202,255 ÷ 60 × 10 = 33,709 for ten months, so its EBIT would be about $39,078 and its interest coverage 2.79 rather than 3.14. EBITDA, $92,587, is the same either way, because both depreciation and interest are added back.

scenes.head: Equity is a residual: assets minus liabilities.

segs.say: Equity is a residual: assets minus liabilities. When a company pays its owners more, over the years, than it earns, or makes large losses, equity can fall below zero, and the company reports a shareholders’ deficit. Starbucks is the best-known example among large companies.
Starbucks Corporation, FY2024 ($ millions)

scenes.head: A debt-to-equity ratio of −2.09 does not mean Starbucks has negative leverage; it means the ratio has stopped working.

segs.say: A debt-to-equity ratio of −2.09 does not mean Starbucks has negative leverage; it means the ratio has stopped working. As equity approaches zero, debt ÷ equity and the equity multiplier rise without limit, and debt to capital climbs past 100% (Starbucks’ is 191.6%); when equity crosses zero the first two flip sign and any comparison breaks. Return on equity fails the same way. With negative equity, use measures that don’t divide by it: debt ratio, debt to EBITDA and coverage. By those, Starbucks covers its interest 9.62 times and its net debt is 1.72 times EBITDA: a company with heavy obligations that its earnings carry comfortably.

scenes.head: Where the deficit came from matters too.

segs.say: Where the deficit came from matters too. Starbucks already had a shareholders’ deficit of $5,314.5 million at the start of fiscal 2022. Over fiscal 2022 to 2024 it paid $7,280.1 million in dividends and $6,264.1 million to repurchase its own shares, $13,544.2 million in all, against net earnings attributable to Starbucks of $11,167.0 million: $2,377.2 million more than it earned. Paying out more than it earned, financed partly by borrowing, is a choice about capital structure, not a sign of losses. A small business with negative equity from accumulated losses is a very different case, and the debt ratio alone won’t tell them apart: read the statement of changes in equity.

scenes.head: For comparison, Harbourline Roasters, the fictional roaster from F00, has a debt ratio of 54.5%, debt to equity of 0.70, interest coverage of 5.55…

segs.say: For comparison, Harbourline Roasters, the fictional roaster from F00, has a debt ratio of 54.5%, debt to equity of 0.70, interest coverage of 5.55 and net debt of 1.77 times EBITDA, close to Lantern’s 2026 leverage but with much weaker coverage.

scenes.head: Debt ratio (total liabilities to total assets)

segs.say: Debt ratio (total liabilities to total assets): Debt ratio = (Total liabilities)/(Total assets).
Total liabilities: Everything the business owes, current and noncurrent, including lease liabilities ($).
Total assets: Total assets on the same balance sheet ($).
Shown as a percentage. Lantern: 54.8% (2026), 80.8% (2027). Above 100% means negative equity.

scenes.head: Liabilities to equity

segs.say: Liabilities to equity: Liabilities to equity = (Total liabilities)/Equity.
Total liabilities: Everything the business owes ($).
Equity: Total shareholders’ equity ($).
Some textbooks call this the debt-to-equity ratio. Lantern 2027: 265,065 ÷ 62,818 = 4.22.

scenes.head: Debt to equity (interest-bearing debt)

segs.say: Debt to equity (interest-bearing debt): Debt to equity = Debt/Equity.
Debt: Interest-bearing debt: notes, loans, instalment notes, drawn credit lines and their current portions (add lease liabilities only as a stated adjustment) ($).
Equity: Total shareholders’ equity ($).
It assumes this: Equity is positive; with negative equity the ratio is not meaningful.

scenes.head: Debt to capital

segs.say: Debt to capital: Debt to capital = Debt/(Debt + Equity).
Debt: Interest-bearing debt, as above ($).
Equity: Total shareholders’ equity ($).

scenes.head: Equity multiplier

segs.say: Equity multiplier: Equity multiplier = (Total assets)/Equity = 1 + (Total liabilities)/Equity.
Total assets: Total assets ($).
Equity: Total shareholders’ equity ($).
Here on closing balances; DuPont analysis (module 3) uses averages. Lantern: 2.21 (2026), 5.22 (2027).

scenes.head: Interest coverage (times interest earned)

segs.say: Interest coverage (times interest earned): Interest coverage = EBIT/(Interest expense).
EBIT: Earnings before interest and taxes; for a business with no non-operating items, operating income ($).
Interest expense: Interest expense for the same period (it excludes the interest inside an operating lease cost under US GAAP) ($).
Lantern: 31.43 (2026), 11.39 (2027); 3.14 with leases treated as debt.

scenes.head: EBITDA coverage

segs.say: EBITDA coverage: EBITDA coverage = (EBIT + D&A)/(Interest expense).
EBIT + D&A: EBITDA: EBIT plus depreciation and amortisation ($).
Interest expense: Interest expense for the same period ($).

scenes.head: Net debt to EBITDA

segs.say: Net debt to EBITDA: Net debt to EBITDA = (Debt − Cash)/(EBIT + D&A).
Debt − Cash: Net debt: interest-bearing debt less cash and short-term investments ($).
EBIT + D&A: EBITDA for a twelve-month period (annualise a part-year) ($).
It assumes this: Debt and EBITDA on the same basis: if lease liabilities are added to debt, add the lease cost back to EBITDA.
In years: how long EBITDA would take to repay net debt. Lantern 2027: 1.12; 2.51 with leases as debt.

scenes.head: Lease-adjusted debt and EBITDA (US GAAP operating leases)

segs.say: Lease-adjusted debt and EBITDA (US GAAP operating leases): Debt_(adj) = Debt + Lease liabilities, EBITDA_(adj) = EBITDA + Operating lease cost.
Lease liabilities: Current and noncurrent operating lease liabilities ($).
Operating lease cost: The straight-line lease expense in operating income: its interest part moves to interest expense, its amortisation part to D&A ($).

chapters.title: Example: Lantern’s leverage, two year ends

scenes.head: Lantern’s leverage, two year ends

segs.say: From Lantern’s balance sheets: total assets $93,676 and $327,883; total liabilities $51,289 and $265,065; equity $42,387 and $62,818; interest-bearing debt $30,000 and $65,250. Calculate the debt ratio, liabilities to equity, debt to equity and the equity multiplier for both year ends.

scenes.head: Lantern’s leverage, two year ends

segs.say: Step 3. Debt to equity (interest-bearing debt only): 30,000 ÷ 42,387 = 0.71; 65,250 ÷ 62,818 = 1.04.

scenes.head: Lantern’s leverage, two year ends

segs.say: Measured by all liabilities, Lantern’s leverage more than tripled; measured by interest-bearing debt, it rose by about half. The gap between the two is the leases, which is why the next example adjusts for them.

chapters.title: Example: Leases as debt, done consistently

scenes.head: Leases as debt, done consistently

segs.say: Restate Lantern’s 2027 debt to equity, interest coverage and net debt to EBITDA treating the cafés’ operating leases as debt. Lease liabilities are $173,379 at 31 December 2027; the $40,000 lease cost for the year includes $11,124 of interest on the liability. EBIT is $32,787, depreciation $19,800, interest expense $2,879, debt $65,250, cash $6,531, equity $62,818.

scenes.head: Leases as debt, done consistently

segs.say: Step 2. Split the lease cost: interest 11,124; amortisation 40,000 − 11,124 = 28,876.

Step 3. Earnings and interest on the loan basis: EBIT 32,787 + 11,124 = 43,911 (the interest is no longer an operating cost); interest expense 2,879 + 11,124 = 14,003; coverage 43,911 ÷ 14,003 = 3.14.
Step 4. EBITDA: 43,911 + 19,800 + 28,876 = 92,587, which is the reported 52,587 plus the whole 40,000 lease cost. Net debt 238,629 − 6,531 = 232,098; net debt ÷ EBITDA 232,098 ÷ 92,587 = 2.51.
Step 5. The inconsistent version, leases in debt but EBITDA after the lease cost, gives 232,098 ÷ 52,587 = 4.41: it counts the leases as debt without giving back the earnings that pay for them.

scenes.head: Leases as debt, done consistently

segs.say: With leases as debt: debt to equity 3.80, interest coverage 3.14, net debt to EBITDA 2.51 (not 4.41).

Treated as financing, the cafés make Lantern a heavily leveraged business whose earnings cover its financing costs about three times. That is the comparison a lender would make with a café owner who borrowed to buy its premises.

chapters.title: Example: How much more can Lantern borrow?

scenes.head: How much more can Lantern borrow?

segs.say: Before accepting Coastline’s 2028 offer, Ana asks Pembury Bank, a fictional lender, for a quote on a $60,000 five-year loan for the 2028 expansion. Pembury’s term sheet allows net debt of at most 3.0 times EBITDA and defines debt to include lease liabilities. Using 2027’s figures, how much headroom does Lantern have, and would the loan fit? Assume the loan is spent on the kitchen, so cash does not rise.

scenes.head: How much more can Lantern borrow?

segs.say: Step 1. Without leases (for comparison): maximum net debt 3.0 × 52,587 = 157,761; headroom 157,761 − 58,719 = 99,042. After the loan: (58,719 + 60,000) ÷ 52,587 = 2.26. It fits.
Step 2. With leases, and EBITDA before the lease cost: maximum 3.0 × 92,587 = 277,761; headroom 277,761 − 232,098 = 45,663. After the loan: 292,098 ÷ 92,587 = 3.15. It doesn’t fit.
Step 3. With leases in debt but EBITDA after the lease cost, Lantern would already be at 4.41 and the loan would take it to 292,098 ÷ 52,587 = 5.55.

Step 4. Judgement: under Pembury’s definition the loan is about $14,000 too large on 2027’s earnings. Ana could borrow about $45,000, wait for a year of full café earnings (2027 had only ten months of them), or ask that the definition match debt with EBITDA before lease costs, which the term sheet must state explicitly.

scenes.head: How much more can Lantern borrow?

segs.say: Headroom is $45,663 under a lease-inclusive definition with matching EBITDA, so a $60,000 loan would take Lantern to 3.15, over the 3.0 limit; without leases it would be 2.26 and fit easily.
The same business passes or fails depending on how the agreement defines debt and EBITDA. Read the definitions before the numbers, and test a loan on the figures after the borrowing, not before it.

scenes.head: Solvency and leverage: Lantern, Starbucks and Harbourline

segs.say: Lantern’s two year ends beside Starbucks and the fictional Harbourline. Tick “Count operating lease liabilities as debt”: Lantern’s 2027 debt to equity rises to 3.80, and because the widget restates EBIT, interest and EBITDA on the same basis, coverage falls to 3.14 and net debt to EBITDA rises to 2.51 (not the mismatched 4.41). Starbucks’ debt to equity shows why negative equity breaks the ratio. Pause the video and try it in the Explore section of this lesson.

scenes.head: Leverage ratios as equity shrinks

segs.say: Change the balance sheet and watch the leverage ratios. Lower total assets until equity approaches zero: liabilities to equity and the equity multiplier explode, then become meaningless below zero, while the debt ratio keeps telling a sensible story. Pause the video and try it in the Explore section of this lesson.

scenes.head: “Debt to equity and liabilities to equity are the same ratio.”

segs.say: “Debt to equity and liabilities to equity are the same ratio.”. They share a denominator, not a numerator. Lantern’s 2027 liabilities to equity is 4.22; its interest-bearing debt to equity is 1.04. Textbooks and data providers use both names loosely, so state your definition and use the same one for every company you compare.

scenes.head: “Operating leases aren’t debt because the payments are operating expenses.”

segs.say: “Operating leases aren’t debt because the payments are operating expenses.”. The payments are as fixed as a loan’s, and since ASC 842 the obligation is on the balance sheet. Counting the liability as debt is a choice, but leaving it out treats Lantern as if it owned its cafés outright. Show the ratios both ways when leases are large.

scenes.head: “Add the leases to debt and keep EBITDA as reported.”

segs.say: “Add the leases to debt and keep EBITDA as reported.”. That puts the leases in the numerator and their cost in the denominator too: Lantern’s net debt to EBITDA comes out at 4.41 instead of 2.51. If the lease is debt, its cost is financing: add the lease cost back to EBITDA, and move its interest part into interest expense for coverage.

scenes.head: Using net income for interest coverage

segs.say: Using net income for interest coverage. Net income is after interest and tax, so it understates what is available to pay interest: 22,431 ÷ 2,879 = 7.79 instead of 11.39 for Lantern. Use EBIT, the earnings before the interest you are testing.

scenes.head: “Negative debt to equity means low leverage.”

segs.say: “Negative debt to equity means low leverage.”. Starbucks’ −2.09 comes from negative equity, a shareholders’ deficit, not from negative debt. When equity is negative or tiny, debt to equity, the equity multiplier and return on equity are not meaningful; use the debt ratio, debt to EBITDA and coverage instead.

scenes.head: “High interest coverage means the debt is safe.”

segs.say: “High interest coverage means the debt is safe.”. Coverage ignores principal. Lantern covers its 2027 interest 11.39 times but $51,091 of its debt principal falls due in 2028, and its lease payments as well. Look at the repayment schedule and the cash flow that will meet it.

scenes.head: Coastline’s credit review, continued.

segs.say: Coastline’s credit review, continued. The credit officer records Lantern’s leverage both ways and writes one sentence on each. Excluding leases, Lantern is moderately geared (debt to equity 1.04, net debt 1.12 times EBITDA) and covers its interest more than eleven times. Including leases, it is heavily geared (3.80, and 2.51 times lease-adjusted EBITDA) with coverage of about three times. She notes that most of the interest-bearing debt is short-term (the line of credit, the Coastline note and the brewer plan’s 2028 payments) and that the business will need to refinance part of it in 2028, which links solvency back to the liquidity review.

scenes.head: Ana’s capital structure.

segs.say: Ana’s capital structure. Ana has financed growth almost entirely with borrowing and leases: no new shares in 2027, and a dividend of $2,000. That kept her ownership at 100% but left equity thin. Hollis Avery’s planned investment in 2028 would lower every leverage ratio at once; the question for Ana is the price of that equity against the interest and the covenants of more debt. F05 develops the trade-off; this lesson gives her the measures to see it.

scenes.head: Reading a large company.

segs.say: Reading a large company. An analyst reviewing Starbucks for a bond fund ignores its debt to equity, which is meaningless, and its return on equity, which is too. She looks at coverage (9.62 times), net debt to EBITDA (1.72, before leases) and the size of the lease liabilities, $10,234.7 million, about two-thirds as large as the company’s financial debt. Then she reads the notes for the maturity of both, because a company that pays out more than it earns relies on refinancing each maturity as it falls due.

scenes.head: What to remember

segs.say: Solvency is the ability to meet all obligations over the long run; leverage is financing with borrowed money, which magnifies both gains and losses.
Leverage ratios (debt ratio, liabilities to equity, debt to equity, debt to capital, equity multiplier) compare balances and convert into one another: equity multiplier = 1 + liabilities ÷ equity.
Coverage ratios compare flows: EBIT or EBITDA against interest expense; net debt to EBITDA gives the years of earnings the debt represents. Annualise part-year EBITDA when dividing a balance by it.
Lantern 2026 → 2027: debt ratio 54.8% → 80.8%; debt to equity 0.71 → 1.04; interest coverage 31.43 → 11.39; net debt −$12,940 → $58,719 (1.12 times EBITDA).
Vendor finance, such as Lantern’s brewer plan at an implied 4.73%, is interest-bearing debt and belongs with the bank loans.

Operating lease liabilities are on the balance sheet under ASC 842; counting them as debt is a judgement that must be applied consistently: add the lease cost back to EBITDA and its interest to interest expense. Lantern: debt to equity 3.80, coverage 3.14, net debt to EBITDA 2.51.
With negative equity (Starbucks: a deficit of $7,441.6 million), debt to equity and ROE are meaningless; use the debt ratio, debt to EBITDA and coverage.

scenes.head: Work the guided problems, then take the knowledge check.

segs.say: That is the whole lesson. Now work the guided problems, with hints when you need them, then try the questions on your own and take the knowledge check. A score of 80 percent completes the lesson.
